lead: A closed traverse should return to its start. In practice it lands a small distance away. That gap is the closing error. Surveyors measure it, compare it with the perimeter, and spread it over the lines by a fixed rule so the traverse closes exactly. The same arithmetic turns field angles and distances into one consistent set of coordinates for maps, land records, road alignment and GIS layers.
prereq: You need traverse surveying: latitudes and departures for latitudes, departures and coordinates, and compass surveying and local attraction for angular misclosure.

sections.h3: The closing error and what it tells you

blocks.text: Run a closed traverse from A through B, C, D and back toward A. The computed last point is A′, not exactly A. From A to A′ the displacement has two parts: the sum of latitudes ΣL and the sum of departures ΣD. In a perfect close both are zero.

blocks.where: e is the closing error in metres; ΣL is the algebraic sum of latitudes in metres, north positive and south negative; ΣD is the algebraic sum of departures in metres, east positive and west negative.

θ is the acute angle from the north–south line. Choose the quadrant from the signs: ΣL positive and ΣD positive gives north-east; ΣL negative and ΣD positive gives south-east; both negative gives south-west; ΣL positive and ΣD negative gives north-west.

blocks.text: With ΣL = −0.23 m and ΣD = −0.12 m, tan θ = 0.12/0.23 = 0.522, so θ = 27°33′. Both sums are negative, so A′ lies south-west of A. The bearing from A to A′ is 180° + 27°33′ = 207°33′.

Size alone is not enough. A 0.4 m error in a 100 m loop is serious; in a 10 km loop it is small. Compare with relative precision: P ÷ e, where P = Σlᵢ is the perimeter in metres and e is the closing error in metres. Write it as 1 in P/e. A rough compass traverse is accepted at a much lower precision (1 in a few hundred to about 1 in 1000) than a theodolite or total station traverse (1 in several thousand or better). Always use the limit set for the job.

sections.h3: Angular and linear misclosure; Bowditch rule

blocks.text: Two different misclosures exist. Angular misclosure compares the measured angles with geometry. For a closed polygon of n sides, the interior angles must sum to (2n − 4) × 90°. For n = 5 the sum is 540°. The observed sum minus this value is the angular misclosure.

Correct large angular misclosure first. Otherwise every bearing, and so every latitude and departure, carries the same error. Linear misclosure is e above, in metres, computed after the latitudes and departures.
The Bowditch rule, also called the compass rule, spreads the linear misclosure in proportion to line length. For line i of length lᵢ:

blocks.where: C<sub>Li</sub> is the correction to latitude in metres; C<sub>Di</sub> is the correction to departure in metres; ΣL and ΣD are the misclosures in metres; lᵢ is the length of line i in metres; P is the perimeter in metres.

blocks.text: The minus sign is essential: corrections act opposite to the misclosure. Add C<sub>Li</sub> to the latitude of line i and C<sub>Di</sub> to its departure. Then add the adjusted latitudes and departures cumulatively from station to station to get coordinates. The new sums must be zero, apart from rounding.

Why Bowditch for compass work? A compass bearing is less precise than a theodolite angle, and its effect on a line's latitude and departure grows with the line's length. Distance error also grows with length. The rule puts more correction on longer lines. That is a reasonable simple model, not a physical law.

The transit rule is the alternative: correction to latitude proportional to |latitude|, and to departure proportional to |departure|, not to length. It suits a theodolite traverse, where angles are more precise than distances. The equal rule gives every line the same correction. Least-squares adjustment is the rigorous method; it is taught with weights and adjustment of observations in control surveys.

Some syllabi add omitted measurements. One length or one bearing of a closed traverse is missing. Use ΣL = 0 and ΣD = 0. If line i has unknown length l and bearing θ, the known lines give ΣL<sub>known</sub> and ΣD<sub>known</sub>. The components of the missing line are therefore l cos θ = −ΣL<sub>known</sub> and l sin θ = −ΣD<sub>known</sub>.

Square and add: l = √(ΣL<sub>known</sub>² + ΣD<sub>known</sub>²). Divide: tan θ = ΣD<sub>known</sub> ÷ ΣL<sub>known</sub>. Take the quadrant from the signs of the components of the missing line, that is from −ΣL<sub>known</sub> (its latitude) and −ΣD<sub>known</sub> (its departure), not from the signs of the sums themselves.

Example: in the traverse of the worked example below, suppose the length and bearing of DA were not recorded. The three known lines give ΣL<sub>known</sub> = 141.42 − 127.28 − 138.56 = −124.42 m and ΣD<sub>known</sub> = 141.42 + 127.28 − 80.00 = +188.70 m. So DA has latitude +124.42 m and departure −188.70 m: north-west. l = √(124.42² + 188.70²) = 226.03 m; tan α = 188.70/124.42 = 1.517, α = 56°36′, so the bearing is 360° − 56°36′ = 303°24′. The missing line absorbs the whole misclosure, which is why an omitted measurement leaves no check.

Check by recomputing both sums. Two omitted quantities, one on each of two lines, can still be solved from ΣL = 0 and ΣD = 0: two unknown lengths give two linear equations, and two unknown bearings give two simultaneous equations for the directions. If three or more quantities are missing, the two closing equations are not enough. You need extra field data or least squares. Do not guess.

examples.question: The closed compass traverse ABCD of the latitude and departure chapter has AB = 200 m at 45°, BC = 180 m at 135°, CD = 160 m at 210° and DA = 226 m at 303°20′, so ΣL = −0.23 m and ΣD = −0.12 m. Find the closing error, its bearing and the relative precision. Adjust the traverse by the Bowditch rule and give the coordinates of A, B, C and D, taking A as (1000.00 E, 1000.00 N).
steps: Bearing: tan θ = 0.12/0.23 = 0.522, θ = 27°33′. Both sums are negative, so A′ is south-west of A: bearing 180° + 27°33′ = 207°33′.
Perimeter P = 200 + 180 + 160 + 226 = 766 m. Relative precision = 766/0.259 = 2953, so about 1 in 2950.
Latitude corrections C<sub>L</sub> = +0.23 × l/766: AB +0.060, BC +0.054, CD +0.048, DA +0.068 m; sum +0.230 m.
Departure corrections C<sub>D</sub> = +0.12 × l/766: AB +0.031, BC +0.028, CD +0.025, DA +0.036 m (the last rounded up 1 mm so the sum is exactly +0.120 m).
Adjusted latitudes: AB +141.480, BC −127.226, CD −138.512, DA +124.258 m (sum 0.000). Adjusted departures: AB +141.451, BC +127.308, CD −79.975, DA −188.784 m (sum 0.000).
examples.answer: Closing error 0.259 m at 207°33′, relative precision about 1 in 2950; adjusted coordinates A (1000.00, 1000.00), B (1141.45, 1141.48), C (1268.76, 1014.25), D (1188.78, 875.74), in metres east and north.

traps: Dividing the misclosure by the number of lines in the Bowditch rule. The denominator is the perimeter P = Σlᵢ; a longer line must receive a larger share.
Using C<sub>L</sub> = +ΣL(l/P). The correct sign is minus; when ΣL itself is negative the correction becomes positive. A same-direction correction doubles the error instead of removing it.
Reporting θ = 29° from tan θ = 0.19/0.34 while both sums are negative. A′ is south-west of A, so the bearing is 209°, not 29°.
Mixing angular misclosure (degrees) with linear misclosure (metres). Check them separately, and correct large angular error before computing coordinates.
Writing relative precision as e/P. It is P/e, expressed as 1 in P/e; a larger number after '1 in' means a better traverse.

quiz.q: State the closing error formula for a closed traverse and define ΣL and ΣD.
quiz.a: e = √((ΣL)² + (ΣD)²). ΣL is the algebraic sum of latitudes in metres, north positive and south negative. ΣD is the algebraic sum of departures in metres, east positive and west negative.

quiz.q: Why is the Bowditch rule commonly used for compass traverses?
quiz.a: Compass bearings are imprecise, and their positional effect grows with line length; distance errors also grow with length. Bowditch spreads the misclosure in proportion to length, so longer, less reliable lines get larger corrections. It is a simple model, not a physical law.

quiz.q: A closed traverse has ΣL = +0.24 m, ΣD = −0.18 m and perimeter 1200 m. Find e, the bearing quadrant and relative precision.
quiz.a: e = √(0.24² + 0.18²) = 0.30 m. tan θ = 0.18/0.24 = 0.75, θ = 36.9°. ΣL positive and ΣD negative gives north-west, bearing 360° − 36.9° = 323.1°. Relative precision = 1200/0.30 = 4000, about 1 in 4000.

quiz.q: A student uses C<sub>L</sub> = +ΣL(l/P) instead of −ΣL(l/P). What happens to the adjusted latitude sum?
quiz.a: Every correction has the wrong sign, so the adjusted sum becomes ΣL + ΣL = 2ΣL, not zero. The misclosure is doubled, not removed.

quiz.q: What is the sum of interior angles of a closed five-sided polygon?
For a line 250 m long in a traverse of perimeter 2000 m, ΣL = −0.40 m and ΣD = +0.20 m. Find the Bowditch corrections.
When would you choose the transit rule over Bowditch?
quiz.a: When angles are more precise than distances, as in a theodolite traverse. Transit corrections follow the size of latitude and departure rather than line length.

quiz.q: How does angular misclosure differ from linear misclosure?
quiz.a: Angular misclosure is the difference between measured angles and the geometric sum, in angle units. Linear misclosure is the gap e between start and computed end, in metres. Correct angles first, then adjust the linear misclosure.

beyond: Not for the exam. Total stations and GNSS log coordinates directly, and software runs a least squares adjustment using weights from instrument specifications. The same closure checks appear in GIS traverse tools and cadastral software. Search for 'traverse adjustment Bowditch', 'transit rule' and 'loop closure total station' to go further.
